prompt:
Write a technical description of about 1,000 words of what happens between a browser being given an HTTPS address and the first byte of the response arriving. The reader is a junior web developer.

Write it as plain prose with no headings or lists. Let the length of each sentence follow what it has to say. Do not use a short sentence to set up a longer one.
context_note: Prompt sent as the subagent's whole task. The subagent also carried the Claude Code agent system prompt, tool definitions and CLAUDE.md.
sampling: harness defaults; not set by the experimenter
text:
When you give a browser an HTTPS address such as https://www.example.com/shop?id=7, the first thing it does is parse the string into a scheme (https, which implies port 443), a host (www.example.com), a path and a query, and then decide whether it needs the network at all. It checks its HSTS list to see whether the host must be reached over HTTPS even if you had typed http, it looks for a service worker registered for that origin that might answer the request itself, and it consults the HTTP cache, where a still-fresh stored copy is returned immediately and nothing below this point happens. Only when none of these short-circuits applies does the browser start looking for a server.

The browser knows the hostname but the network speaks in IP addresses, so DNS resolution comes next. The browser checks its own DNS cache, then asks the operating system, which checks its cache and the hosts file, and finally the OS sends a query to a configured recursive resolver, usually run by your ISP, your router or a public provider. If the resolver has no cached answer it works down the hierarchy, asking a root server which servers handle .com, asking those which servers are authoritative for example.com, and asking those for the A record (IPv4) or AAAA record (IPv6) of www.example.com. Every record carries a time-to-live that tells each cache how long it may keep the answer, which is why a DNS change can take a while to be seen everywhere. Many sites also publish a CNAME, an alias that adds another lookup, and modern browsers may query for HTTPS records or use DNS over HTTPS so that the lookup is encrypted. Resolution often takes from a few milliseconds when cached to a few hundred when it is not, and it is a common hidden contributor to slow first loads.

With an IP address in hand the browser opens a TCP connection to port 443, which begins with the three-way handshake: the client sends a SYN, the server answers SYN-ACK, and the client confirms with ACK, costing one full round trip before any application data can flow. If the browser and server both support HTTP/3, the transport is instead QUIC running over UDP, which folds the transport and encryption handshakes together and saves round trips, but a browser usually learns that a server offers HTTP/3 from a previous HTTP/2 response header (Alt-Svc) or a DNS record, so your first visit to a site commonly still goes over TCP. Browsers will also race IPv6 against IPv4 and fall back quickly, a behaviour called Happy Eyeballs, so a broken IPv6 path does not stall you.

On top of the connection comes the TLS handshake, which is what makes the address an HTTPS one. In TLS 1.3 the client sends a ClientHello listing the cipher suites it supports, a key share for an ephemeral Diffie-Hellman exchange, the Server Name Indication naming www.example.com so a server hosting many sites knows which certificate to present, and the protocols it can speak via ALPN, typically h2 and http/1.1. The server replies with its chosen cipher and its own key share, after which both sides can compute the same shared secret without ever sending it, and everything the server sends from then on is encrypted, including its certificate. The browser validates that certificate by checking that it names the host you asked for, that it has not expired, that its signature chains up through intermediate certificates to a root authority already trusted by your operating system or browser, and that it has not been revoked, which is checked through mechanisms such as stapled OCSP responses or the browser's own revocation lists. If any check fails you see the full-page warning rather than the site, because continuing would mean you could be talking to an impostor. When both sides finish by exchanging Finished messages, which prove that neither saw a tampered handshake, the channel is ready, and TLS 1.3 needs only one additional round trip for all of this, or none when resuming a session with a previously issued ticket. Older TLS 1.2 needs two round trips, which is part of why upgrading matters.

Now the browser can finally send an HTTP request, and the ALPN result decides its shape. Over HTTP/1.1 it is readable text: a request line such as GET /shop?id=7 HTTP/1.1 followed by headers like Host, User-Agent, Accept, Accept-Encoding and Accept-Language, and then a blank line. Over HTTP/2 the same information travels as compressed binary frames on a numbered stream, which lets many requests share one connection instead of waiting in line. The browser also attaches any cookies it holds for that origin and may include conditional headers such as If-None-Match, carrying an ETag from a stale cached copy so the server can reply with a tiny 304 Not Modified instead of resending the whole body. Because the request is encrypted, someone watching the network can see the destination IP address and, unless Encrypted Client Hello is in use, the hostname from the SNI field, but not the path, query or cookies.

The request then crosses the internet, which is a chain of routers each forwarding packets by looking at the destination address, and frequently it does not reach the site's own machine at all but a CDN edge or load balancer chosen by DNS or anycast routing to be geographically near you. That front end may terminate TLS itself, serve a cached response, or forward the request on to an application server, which in turn may query a database, call other services, render a template and assemble a response. All of that server-side work, together with the network travel in each direction, is what you perceive as waiting.

The moment of interest is the arrival of the first byte of the response, which is the start of the status line and headers (for example HTTP/2 200 with a content-type) travelling back down the same encrypted connection, and the interval from sending the request to that moment is what the developer tools call Time To First Byte. It is really the sum of everything above: DNS, connection setup, TLS, the request's flight, the server's processing time and the response's flight back. This is why the usual fixes for a slow first byte are to cache aggressively, put content on a CDN, reuse connections with keep-alive, enable HTTP/2 or 3 and TLS 1.3, and keep server work short, and it is why the Network panel's timing breakdown, which separates these phases, is the right place to look when you need to know which one is costing you.
